t: The FAIR Plan's 29% Rate Increase Is Here: What It Means for Your Mortgage Payment
c: FAIR Plan premiums jumped an average 29.1% on October 15. Here's how it reaches your mortgage payment, and what you can do about it.
x: The short answer: On October 15, 2026, California FAIR Plan premiums rose an average of 29.1% for new and renewing policies, the largest increase in the plan's recent history. If your insurance is paid through your mortgage escrow account, the higher premium will show up in your monthly payment after your servicer's next escrow review. Homes in high wildfire-risk areas will see the biggest jumps, some lower-risk homes will see decreases, and wildfire-mitigation discounts and a fresh look at the private market are the best ways to soften the hit. As of October 18, 2026. What exactly changed on October 15? The FAIR Plan, California's insurer of last resort, asked the Department of Insurance in September 2025 for an average 35.8% increase on its homeowner (dwelling) policies. The Department approved an average of 29.1% (the Department's own summary rounds it to 29% versus 36% requested), effective October 15, 2026 for new and renewing policies ( CDI, May 20, 2026 ; KQED, August 11, 2026 ). "Average" is doing a lot of work in that number. According to reporting on the filing, the increase is concentrated in the wildfire portion of the premium: homes in fire-prone areas pay the most, some wildfire premiums will double, and some lower-risk urban policyholders will see decreases ( KQED ; Salinas Californian via Yahoo Finance, May 22, 2026 ). In parts of Los Angeles County like Malibu, and in mountain communities like Lake Arrowhead, about half of homes are insured through the FAIR Plan, KQED reported. How will the FAIR Plan increase affect my monthly mortgage payment? If you have an escrow (impound) account, your servicer pays your insurance and property taxes for you and collects the cost in your monthly payment. Federal rules (RESPA's Regulation X) require your servicer to review the account at least once a year and send you an annual statement ( 12 CFR 1024.17 ). When your renewal premium goes up, the next review will usually show two things: A higher monthly escrow amount going forward, to cover the new premium. A shortage , if the account paid a bigger bill than it collected for. If the shortage is one month's escrow payment or more, the servicer can leave it alone or spread repayment over at least 12 months; it cannot demand a lump sum. Smaller shortages can be billed within 30 days. You can always choose to pay a shortage early to keep the monthly amount lower. The servicer can also hold a cushion of up to one-sixth of a year's escrow disbursements, so the cushion grows when the premium does. A hypothetical, for scale: if a FAIR Plan premium of $3,000 a year rose by exactly the 29.1% average, it would become about $3,873, or roughly $73 more per month through escrow, before any shortage or cushion adjustment. Your actual premium change could be much higher or lower. If you pay your insurance yourself (no escrow), you'll see the change directly on your renewal bill. Just make sure it's paid on time: if coverage lapses, your servicer can buy "force-placed" insurance for you, which is typically expensive and covers less. Does my lender accept FAIR Plan coverage? In my experience, yes, as long as the total coverage meets the investor's rules. For a Fannie Mae loan on a one-to-four-unit home, the property must be insured on a replacement-cost basis, the deductible can't exceed 5% of the coverage amount, and if one policy leaves out a required peril, the borrower has to add another policy to fill the gap ( Fannie Mae Selling Guide B7-3-02 ). That last point matters here. The FAIR Plan's dwelling policy is a named-peril policy covering fire, lightning, internal explosion and smoke ( California FAIR Plan ). It doesn't cover water damage, theft or liability. Those come from a separate Difference in Conditions (DIC) policy, which the FAIR Plan doesn't sell ( California FAIR Plan, DIC ). The Department of Insurance says only about half of FAIR Plan policyholders carry one ( CDI fact sheet ). So when your FAIR Plan premium rises, remember

t: LA's Prop TE on the November Ballot: What It Means for Palisades Fire Homeowners Who Sell
c: A plain-English, neutral guide to Prop TE: who would qualify for the ULA exemption, what it could save, and what each side says.
x: The short answer: Proposition TE, on the City of Los Angeles ballot on November 3, 2026, would give a one-time exemption from Measure ULA (the city's "mansion tax") to residential properties damaged or destroyed in the January 2025 Palisades Fire, when they are sold by the person who owned them on the day the fire started, through January 6, 2030. It matters only for sales above the ULA threshold, currently $5.4 million, where the tax is 4% or 5.5% of the price. It would also allow refunds for qualifying owners who already paid, and it needs a simple majority to pass. As of October 17, 2026. This article explains the measure; it does not recommend a vote. What is Measure ULA, and how much is it today? Voters approved Measure ULA in 2022. It is an extra transfer tax on sales of real estate in the City of Los Angeles above a value threshold, and the money goes to the House LA Fund for affordable housing and tenant assistance. The thresholds adjust every year for inflation. According to the LA Office of Finance, for sales closing after June 30, 2026: $5.4 million or less: no ULA tax (the city's regular 0.45% transfer tax still applies) Over $5.4 million and under $10.9 million: 4% ULA tax, or 4.45% combined with the regular tax $10.9 million or more: 5.5% ULA tax, or 5.95% combined One detail many sellers miss: ULA is figured on the gross value of the sale, and the rate applies to the entire price, not just the part above the threshold. A hypothetical, for scale: a qualifying lot or damaged home that sells for $6 million would owe $240,000 in ULA tax (4% of $6 million) under current rules. Under Prop TE, a qualifying seller would not owe that ULA amount. The regular city transfer tax would still apply. What exactly would Prop TE change? Per the City's official Voter Information Pamphlet, Prop TE would: Exempt sales of residential properties damaged or destroyed in the Palisades Fire from the ULA tax. Apply only when the seller is the owner on January 7, 2025 , the day the fire started. Cover sales from January 7, 2025 through January 6, 2030 (five years from the fire). Allow refunds of ULA tax already paid on qualifying sales. It does not repeal or change ULA for anyone else. Buyers who later resell those properties would be back under the normal rules. The Chief Legislative Analyst's summary notes the fire damaged or destroyed about 5,620 structures, roughly 5,495 of them residential. Who would qualify, and who wouldn't? ULA is a City of Los Angeles tax, so it doesn't apply to properties in other cities or unincorporated areas. Whether a particular parcel "was damaged or destroyed" and how the exemption is claimed would be handled by the city if the measure passes, so confirm with the Office of Finance and your escrow officer before you count on it. What do supporters and critics say? Supporters (the ballot argument is signed by Mayor Karen Bass, Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson, Councilmember Traci Park, whose district includes the Palisades, and others, including state legislators and building-trades and Palisades community leaders) argue that ULA "was never intended to penalize survivors who lost everything in a declared disaster," that many owners are selling because they have to, and that the exemption is narrow, temporary, and leaves ULA in place. Critics and concerns: No official argument against Prop TE was filed with the City Clerk. When the City Council voted 13–1 to place it on the ballot, Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez voted no, arguing the exemption should have been limited to people whose primary residence burned and who need help rebuilding, rather than also covering LLCs, investors, and owners of several properties. The City Administrative Officer estimates Prop TE would reduce House LA Fund revenue by $35 million to $66 million through January 2030 , money that would otherwise go to affordable housing and tenant assistance. t: Helping Your Adult Child Buy a Home: Gift, Co-Sign, or Co-Borrow?
c: Three ways parents help with a first home, and what each one does to your taxes, your credit and your own borrowing.
x: The short answer: A gift is usually the cleanest way to help. In 2026 you can give each child up to $19,000 ($38,000 from a married couple) without filing a gift tax return, and on a one-unit primary home the entire down payment can be a documented gift. Co-signing or co-borrowing helps your child qualify on income, but the loan shows up on your credit and counts against your own borrowing for years. Decide what you're really solving for: cash for the down payment, or income to qualify. What problem are you actually solving? Most of the parents I talk with in the San Gabriel Valley want to help, but they're solving one of two different problems: Your child has the income but not the down payment. That's a cash problem. A gift solves it. Your child has savings but can't qualify on income alone. That's an income problem. Co-borrowing, or co-signing in some programs, solves it. Mixing these up is how families end up with a parent on a 30-year loan they never needed to be on. How does a gift work? Fannie Mae allows gifts from relatives, a domestic partner, a fiancé or fiancée, or someone with a long-standing family-like relationship. On a one-unit primary residence, your child doesn't have to put in any of their own money; the whole down payment can be a gift ( Fannie Mae B3-4.3-04 ). Two- to four-unit homes and second homes require 5% from the borrower. The lender will want: A gift letter with the amount, a statement that no repayment is expected, and your name, address, phone number and relationship. A paper trail : your check and your child's deposit slip, a wire to your child, or a wire straight to escrow. If the money goes directly to closing, it must be a wire, certified check or cashier's check. Send the money early and in one piece. A gift that sits in your child's account for a couple of months, documented once, is far easier than three transfers a week before closing. Will I owe gift tax? Almost certainly not. The 2026 annual exclusion is $19,000 per recipient , or $38,000 if you and your spouse give together ( IRS gift tax FAQ ). Give more than that to one person in a year and you generally file Form 709 by April 15 of the following year ( IRS Form 709 instructions ). Filing doesn't mean paying: the excess counts against your lifetime exemption, which is $15 million per person in 2026 ( IRS ). Your CPA should file it, but for most families no tax is due. A gift to your child and their spouse can count as two recipients, which doubles the annual amount. Ask your CPA how to structure it. What changes if I co-sign or co-borrow? Both put you on the note, which means you're fully responsible if payments stop. The difference is ownership: Co-signers sign the note but have no ownership interest in the home. Non-occupant co-borrowers share the loan and may or may not be on title ( Fannie Mae B2-2-04 ). The cost to you shows up later. When you go to refinance or buy your next home, that mortgage payment counts against your debt-to-income ratio, unless your child has made every payment from their own account for the most recent 12 months with no late payments, and you can prove it with canceled checks or bank statements ( Fannie Mae B3-6-05 ). Even then, it still counts toward your number of financed properties. If you co-sign, have your child pay from an account in their own name, starting with the first payment. That one habit gives you your borrowing power back after a year. What about a gift of equity? If you're selling a home to your child, you can credit part of your equity toward their down payment and closing costs. It's documented with a gift letter and shows on the settlement statement ( Fannie Mae B3-4.3-05 ). For the family home itself, property tax is a separate question: Prop 19's parent-child rules apply, and I covered them in Inheriting Your Parents' California Home . t: Divorce and the Family Home in California: Keep It, Sell It, or Buy Out Your Spouse?
c: How a spousal buyout really works, why a quitclaim deed doesn't take your ex off the loan, and the tax rules that help.
x: The short answer: In California, a home bought during the marriage is generally community property and is divided equally. If one of you keeps it, the usual route is a refinance that pays out the other spouse's share. Fannie Mae treats that buyout as a limited cash-out refinance, often with better pricing than a regular cash-out. A quitclaim deed changes who owns the house, not who owes the loan, so the refinance is what actually takes your ex off the mortgage. Transfers between spouses in a divorce don't trigger a Prop 13 reassessment. Who owns the house in a California divorce? California is a community property state. What you own or owe together during the marriage is generally divided equally by the judge, and a mortgage taken out during the marriage is community debt that you're both responsible for ( California Courts self-help ). A home one spouse owned before the marriage can stay separate property, but only as long as it was kept separate. Paying down that mortgage with income earned during the marriage can give the other spouse a claim. That's a question for your family law attorney. What are the options for the house? There are three, and each has a different financing picture: One spouse keeps it and buys out the other. The most common path when there are children in school or a low property tax base worth keeping. Sell and split the proceeds. The cleanest break, and often the right answer when neither spouse can qualify alone. Keep owning it together for a set period. Sometimes used until the youngest child finishes school. It keeps both of you on the loan and tied together financially, so it needs a very clear written agreement. How does a spousal buyout work? Fannie Mae treats buying out a co-owner under a divorce as a limited cash-out refinance , not a regular cash-out, when ( Fannie Mae B2-1.3-02 ): you've owned the home jointly for at least 12 months before the new loan, there's a written agreement stating the terms of the transfer and how the money is used, and the spouse keeping the home doesn't take any of the proceeds themselves. The spouse who keeps the home must qualify on their own income. That's often the hardest part, and it's where planning ahead pays off. Can alimony or child support help me qualify? Yes, if it's documented. The lender needs proof of full, regular, on-time payments for the most recent 6 months , and the payments must continue for at least 3 years from the application date ( Fannie Mae B3-3.4-02 ). If your support ends when your youngest turns 18 in two years, it generally can't count. Tell your attorney early if you'll need support income to qualify; the timing and wording of the agreement matter. Can't I just quitclaim the house to my spouse? A quitclaim deed changes ownership , not liability . If your ex keeps the house and you stay on the loan, a late payment hurts your credit, and that payment counts against you when you try to buy your next home. Federal law does keep the lender from calling the loan due when a divorce decree transfers the home to a spouse ( 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3 ), but the original borrower isn't released unless the lender approves it ( Fannie Mae Servicing Guide D1-4.1-02 ). In practice, a refinance is what gets the departing spouse off the loan. What about property tax and capital gains? Property tax: Transfers between spouses, including those under a divorce settlement or court order, are excluded from reassessment automatically ( California BOE ). The spouse who keeps the home keeps the existing Prop 13 base. Transfer between spouses: Under federal tax law, no gain or loss is recognized on a transfer to a spouse or former spouse that's incident to the divorce, and the receiving spouse keeps the original tax basis ( 26 U.S.C. 1041 ). Selling later: The home-sale exclusion is up to $250,000 of gain for a single filer. t: Building an ADU in California: For Family or Rental Income, and How to Pay for It
c: What California now allows on a single-family lot, how lenders count ADU rent, and four ways to pay for the build.
x: The short answer: California makes ADUs easier to build than almost anywhere in the country. Cities must decide on a complete application within 60 days, can't require you to live on the property, and can't charge impact fees on units of 750 square feet or less. You can pay for one with a HELOC, a renovation loan like Fannie Mae HomeStyle, or a cash-out refinance. Once it's rented, lenders can count up to 75% of the rent, capped at 30% of your qualifying income, when you buy or refinance. Why are so many Californians building ADUs? Because the state made it much easier. ADU permits rose from 1,336 in 2016 to 30,354 in 2024 , and ADUs were more than a quarter of all homes permitted in California in 2024 ( HCD ADU Handbook ). In the San Gabriel Valley, I see three reasons over and over: housing aging parents nearby, giving adult children a place to start, and adding rental income to an expensive home. What does California allow on a single-family lot? From the state's ADU Handbook ( HCD ): Up to three units in total: one ADU converted from existing space, one detached ADU, and one junior ADU (JADU) of 500 square feet or less inside the house. A 60-day decision on a complete application when a home already exists on the lot. No owner-occupancy requirement for an ADU. (A JADU that shares a bathroom with the main house is different.) A guaranteed minimum: cities must allow at least an 800-square-foot ADU with 4-foot side and rear setbacks. No impact fees on 750 square feet or less. Above that, fees are proportional to the size of the main house. Two newer laws are worth knowing. AB 1033 lets cities adopt an ordinance allowing an ADU to be sold separately as a condominium; it isn't automatic, so check your city. SB 9 allows up to two homes, or a lot split, on most single-family lots ( HCD SB 9 fact sheet ). Will an ADU raise my property taxes? Only by the value of the new construction. The assessor adds the ADU's value to your existing assessment; your house and land keep their current Prop 13 base ( Nevada County Assessor , applying statewide new-construction rules). For a long-time owner, that's a big advantage over buying a second property. How do I pay for an ADU? Option How it works Best when HELOC Draw as the build progresses; keeps your first mortgage You have equity and a low first-mortgage rate Fannie Mae HomeStyle Renovation Borrow against the value after the ADU is built; can finance new ADU construction ( Fannie Mae ) Current equity is thin but the finished value is strong Cash-out refinance Replace your mortgage with a larger one Your current rate is already near today's rates Construction loan Short-term loan funded in draws Large detached builds, or when other options don't fit Can ADU rent help me qualify for a loan? Yes, within limits. On a one-unit primary home with one ADU, Fannie Mae lets lenders count rent on a purchase or limited cash-out refinance. The calculation uses 75% of the rent , and ADU income can't exceed 30% of your total qualifying income . The rent has to be supported by the appraiser's rent schedule, and if you have less than a year of landlord experience, the income can only offset the housing payment ( Fannie Mae B3-3.8-02 ). Freddie Mac's rule is similar ( Freddie Mac ADU fact sheet ). That matters most when buying a home that already has a permitted ADU. An unpermitted unit generally can't be counted, and it can complicate the appraisal, so get permits sorted before you sell or refinance. Derek\'s take The ADU conversations I enjoy most are the multigenerational ones: a backyard unit for grandparents, or a first home for a grown child, on land the family already owns. Before you hire a designer, let's look at your equity and your first-mortgage rate together. That usually decides the financing, and the financing often decides the size of the ADU. t: HELOC vs. Cash-Out Refinance: How to Tap Your Equity Without Giving Up a Low Rate
c: Why keeping a low first-mortgage rate usually matters more than the HELOC's rate, and when a cash-out still wins.
x: The short answer: If your first mortgage rate is well below today's rates, a HELOC or fixed second mortgage usually costs less overall than a cash-out refinance, because you only pay today's rates on the new money. A cash-out refinance tends to win when your current rate is already close to today's, when you're borrowing a large share of your equity, or when you want one fixed payment. The right answer comes from your blended rate, not the headline rate. Why does this question matter so much right now? Because most homeowners are sitting on rates they'll never see again. As of mid-2026, about 49% of U.S. mortgages had a rate below 4%, and about 66% were below 5% (FHFA National Mortgage Database data, via Wolf Street ). Meanwhile the national average 30-year fixed rate was 7.40% the week of October 15, 2026 ( Freddie Mac PMMS ). If you're in that first half, refinancing your whole balance to get cash means paying today's rate on money that currently costs you 3%. How do the two options compare? HELOC or home equity loan Cash-out refinance Your first mortgage Stays as is Replaced with a new, larger loan Rate on the new money HELOC: usually variable, priced off the prime rate; home equity loan: fixed Today's first-mortgage rate on the whole balance How much you can borrow Commonly up to 80–90% of value combined, depending on the lender Up to 80% of value on a one-unit primary home (Fannie Mae) Closing costs Often low Similar to any refinance Waiting period Varies by lender Your current loan generally must be 12 months old Sources: Fannie Mae Eligibility Matrix ; Fannie Mae B2-1.3-03 . HELOC limits are typical, not a rule. HELOCs are usually priced as the prime rate plus a margin. The prime rate was 7.00% on October 15, 2026 ( Federal Reserve H.15 ). What's a blended rate, and why does it decide this? Your blended rate is the average rate across everything you owe on the house. Here's a simplified, hypothetical example. Say you owe $600,000 at 3% and need $100,000: Keep the first and add a $100,000 line at a hypothetical 8%: your blended rate is about 3.7% on $700,000. Cash-out refinance all $700,000 at a hypothetical 7.4%: your rate is 7.4% on all of it. The line's rate is higher, but it applies to a much smaller balance. The math flips when your first-mortgage rate is already close to today's rates, or when the cash you need is a large share of the total. This example is illustrative only; it is not a quote or an offer of credit. When does a cash-out refinance still make sense? Your current rate is already near today's market rate. You're consolidating high-rate debt and want one fixed payment you can't redraw. You need more than a lender will allow on a second lien. You want to remove someone from the loan or change the term at the same time. Is home equity interest still tax-deductible? Only if you use the money to buy, build or substantially improve the home that secures the loan, within a $750,000 total mortgage-debt limit ( IRS Publication 936 ). The 2025 tax law made the $750,000 limit permanent ( Congressional Research Service ). A HELOC used for a remodel can qualify; one used to pay off a car generally doesn't. Ask your CPA before you borrow. Derek\'s take The question I hear most is "should I refinance to get cash?" The answer I give most is "probably not your first mortgage." Send me your current statement and how much you need, and I'll show you the blended rate for each option side by side, so you can see the real cost before you decide. t: Self-Employed and Planning to Buy? Start With Next Year's Tax Return
c: The deductions lenders add back, the ones they don't, and a 12-month plan for business owners who want to buy.
x: The short answer: Lenders qualify most self-employed borrowers on the income shown on their last two years of tax returns, not on what the business actually brings in. Some write-offs, like depreciation and business use of your home, get added back. Most others don't. If you plan to buy in the next year or two, talk to your tax preparer and your mortgage broker together before you file. One return with a little less in write-offs can raise your buying power more than a year of saving. How do lenders look at self-employed income? Under Fannie Mae's rules, the standard is two years of personal tax returns, plus business returns where required. Only one year is allowed when the business has existed for five years , you've owned at least 25% of it for those five years, and the lender completes a cash-flow analysis ( Fannie Mae B3-3.5-01 ). The lender also orders your tax transcripts directly from the IRS, using Form 4506-C, so the returns you hand over must match what you filed ( Fannie Mae B3-3.1-02 ). There's no "lender version" of a tax return. Which deductions do lenders add back? For a sole proprietor reporting on Schedule C, Fannie Mae's cash-flow analysis adds back several non-cash or one-time deductions ( Fannie Mae B3-3.6-03 ): Most other expenses you deduct, from supplies to your crew's wages, lower the income a lender can use. That's correct for taxes and expensive for a mortgage. What if my income went down last year? Lenders compare your two years. Rising or steady income is generally averaged. If it declined, Fannie Mae's guidance is to use the lower, more recent figure, averaged over 12 months, and the lender has to document that the income has stabilized ( Fannie Mae income calculator FAQ ). A sharp drop can also raise questions about the business itself, so a short letter explaining it, such as a one-time equipment purchase or a slow season, helps. What if my tax returns don't tell the real story? Bank-statement loans qualify you on 12 or 24 months of deposits instead of tax returns. A typical program applies an expense factor, often 50% of business deposits by default, unless your CPA documents a lower one ( Angel Oak, as one example ). These are non-QM loans: they generally cost more and may carry a prepayment penalty, which I'll always tell you up front. They're a good tool, but planning your returns a year ahead often gets you a better loan. A 12-month plan before you buy Derek\'s take A large share of my clients are self-employed, and the pattern is always the same: great business, conservative tax return, surprised at the pre-approval number. The fix is easy if we start early. Call me before your tax preparer files, and we'll find the balance between saving on taxes and qualifying for the home you want. Frequently asked questions How many years of tax returns do I need if I'm self-employed? Usually two. One year can work if the business has existed for five years and you've owned at least 25% of it that long. Does depreciation hurt my mortgage application? No. Lenders add depreciation back to your income in their cash-flow analysis. Can I get a mortgage without tax returns? Yes, through a bank-statement (non-QM) loan, typically using 12 or 24 months of deposits. Expect a higher rate than a conventional loan. Can I amend my returns to show more income? Amended returns can be used in some cases, but lenders look at them closely and you'll owe the additional tax. Talk to me and your CPA first. t: Worried About AI and Your Job? Here's What It Means for Your Mortgage
c: AI is changing hiring faster than it's cutting jobs. What that means for your mortgage, your HELOC and your next move.
x: The short answer: AI hasn't caused widespread layoffs yet, but it is changing hiring, especially for early-career office jobs. If you own a home, the smartest moves happen while your paycheck is steady: build cash reserves, open a home equity line before you need it, and refinance or buy while your income is easy to document. Lenders approve the job you have today, not the one you'll have next year. What's actually happening with AI and jobs? The honest picture in 2026 is more mixed than the headlines. Overall hiring has held up, and job openings were near a two-year high this spring. The pressure is concentrated at the bottom of the ladder. Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found that employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations, such as software and customer service, fell by double digits after late 2022, while older workers in the same jobs held steady ( Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, 2025 ). In plain terms: AI is less likely to take a seasoned professional's job tomorrow than to change what the job looks like, slow raises in some fields, and make the next job search take longer. For a household with a mortgage, that last part is the one to plan for. How does job uncertainty affect my existing mortgage? It doesn't, directly. Your rate, payment, and terms are locked in by your note. No lender re-checks your employment after closing. What changes is your flexibility : Refinancing requires current, verifiable income. If you're between jobs, you generally can't refinance until you're re-employed and have pay stubs. Home equity lines require the same. Banks often freeze or lower HELOC limits in downturns, but a line that's already open is far easier to keep than a new one is to get. Buying the next home gets harder during a job change. Most lenders want a stable two-year history, and a new field or a new 1099 arrangement can mean waiting. What should I do now, while my income is steady? Know your cushion. Aim for six months of total housing cost (mortgage, taxes, insurance, HOA) in savings. In Los Angeles County that's often $30,000 to $50,000. Open a HELOC you don't plan to use. It's a backup emergency fund. Many have no or low annual fees. Draw nothing unless you need it. Refinance now if the math works. If today's rates beat yours, or you want to remove mortgage insurance, do it while your employer letter and W-2s are clean. Buy on your current income, not your hoped-for raise. Size the payment so it still works if a bonus or commission disappears. If you're thinking of going independent, talk to me before you quit. A W-2 to 1099 switch can pause your borrowing options for up to two years on conventional loans. Bank-statement programs can help, but planning ahead is better. What if I'm laid off and have a mortgage? Call your servicer before you miss a payment, not after. Ask about forbearance and loss-mitigation options; they exist for exactly this. Severance can count as reserves but usually not as qualifying income. Don't drain retirement accounts to make the payment until you've spoken with your servicer and a tax professional. And call me: sometimes the best move is a plan for the next 12 months, not a new loan today. Is AI changing how mortgages are underwritten? Yes, mostly behind the scenes. Automated underwriting has existed for decades; AI is now speeding up document review and income calculation. That helps clean files close faster. It doesn't replace judgment on complicated files: self-employed income, multiple properties, family gifts. That's where a broker who can move your file to a different lender still earns his keep. Derek\'s take In 20 years, I've closed loans through the dot-com bust, 2008, and the pandemic. The people who came through best weren't the ones who guessed the economy right. They were the ones who arranged their options while things were calm. If you'd like a 30-minute review of where you stand, no credit pull, I'm happy to do it. t: Earned Wage Access and Buying a Home: What Tradespeople and Gig Workers Should Know
c: Pay-early apps are everywhere in the trades. Here's how they show up when an underwriter reads your bank statements.
x: The short answer: Earned wage access (EWA) apps let you get paid for hours you've already worked before payday. Used occasionally, they're a reasonable tool. Used every pay period, they show up on the bank statements a lender reviews and can raise questions about cash flow. If you work in the trades or gig economy and want to buy or refinance within a year, the biggest wins come from cleaning up three to twelve months of bank statements and documenting your income the way underwriters expect. What is earned wage access? EWA lets workers draw part of their earned-but-unpaid wages early, through an employer program or a direct-to-consumer app. It's common across construction, landscaping, electrical, pool service and delivery work, where paychecks can lag behind real expenses like fuel, tools and materials. California regulates it more closely than most states. The Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) treats direct-to-consumer EWA as a loan, requires providers to register, and counts "tips" and expedited-transfer fees as charges that must be disclosed up front ( Greenberg Traurig on the DFPI rules ). Registration took effect February 15, 2025 ( Consumer Financial Services Law Monitor ). A federal EWA bill cleared a House committee in July 2026 but is not law ( Beancount, July 2026 ). Does using EWA hurt my chances of getting a mortgage? EWA doesn't appear on your credit report the way a credit card does. But underwriters read your bank statements, usually the last two months for a W-2 borrower and twelve to twenty-four months for a bank-statement loan. What they look for: Frequent advance deposits and repayments. Every pay period, it can read as a household living ahead of its income. Fees. A $3 to $5 fast-transfer fee a few times a month adds up and signals cash strain. Large, unexplained deposits. Anything that isn't payroll may need a letter of explanation. Overdrafts or negative balances. More of a red flag than EWA itself. None of these is an automatic denial. They're simply questions, and fewer questions means a smoother, faster approval. How do lenders count income for tradespeople? It depends on how you're paid: How you're paid What lenders usually want Watch out for W-2 hourly or salary 30 days of pay stubs, 2 years of W-2s Overtime and bonus usually need a 2-year history to count 1099 contractor 2 years of tax returns, year-to-date P&L Heavy write-offs lower your qualifying income Business owner (licensed contractor, pool company) 2 years of personal and business returns Same: deductions that save tax shrink your loan amount Mixed or seasonal Averages over 24 months A slow winter is fine if the two-year average holds For self-employed borrowers whose tax returns understate real income, bank-statement loans qualify you on 12 or 24 months of deposits instead. They typically cost more than conventional loans, which is why clean, consistent deposits matter. A 90-day plan if you want to buy or refinance For employers in the trades If you run a landscaping, electrical or pool-service company, employer-sponsored EWA can be a strong recruiting benefit, especially versions with a free transfer option. Pair it with a simple homeownership workshop. I'm glad to run one for your crew at no cost. Derek\'s take Some of my favorite closings are for people who build and maintain California's homes and finally own one themselves. The income is real; it's just documented differently. Bring me your last two years of returns and three months of statements, and I'll tell you honestly what you qualify for today and what to change to qualify for more. Frequently asked questions Is earned wage access a loan in California? For direct-to-consumer apps, the DFPI treats it as one for regulatory purposes; employer-integrated programs can be treated differently. Will an underwriter make me explain EWA deposits? Possibly, if they're large or frequent. A short letter usually resolves it. Can I buy a home with 1099 income? Yes. Most

t: Buy, Remodel, or Tear Down and Rebuild? A California Homeowner's Decision Guide
c: Three ways to get the home you need, compared on timeline, Prop 13 taxes and financing, with a checklist to pick yours.
x: The short answer: If you love your location and have a low mortgage rate, remodeling usually wins, financed with a HELOC or renovation loan so you keep your first mortgage. If the house itself is the problem (layout, foundation, size) and the lot is valuable, rebuilding can make sense but takes the most cash, time and patience. If the neighborhood or school district no longer fits, buying is the cleaner answer, even at a higher rate. The three paths at a glance Buy a different home Remodel what you have Tear down and rebuild Typical timeline 2–4 months 3–12 months 18–36 months including design and permits Keep your current mortgage rate? No Yes, with a HELOC or second Usually no; construction financing replaces it California property tax (Prop 13) Reassessed on the full purchase price Only the added value of the new construction is assessed; land and existing house keep their base The new house gets a new assessed value; the land generally keeps its base year value Where you live during the work No disruption Often at home, or a short-term rental Rental for 12+ months Cost certainty High: price known at contract Medium: surprises behind walls Lowest: bids, permits and change orders Selling costs Roughly 5–7% of the sale price None None The property-tax row is where California differs most. Under Prop 13, assessors add value only for the new construction, while the land and untouched structure keep their indexed base ( Sacramento County Assessor ; Santa Cruz County Assessor ). Owners who bought decades ago often save thousands a year by staying. Option 1: Buy a different home Pros: Fastest path to the house you want. Known price. No construction risk. Cons: You give up your current rate and your Prop 13 base, and pay selling costs. Homeowners 55 and older may be able to transfer their tax base under Prop 19, which can change the math entirely. Financing: Conventional loans up to $1,249,125 in Los Angeles County for 2026 ( FHFA via Calculated Risk ); jumbo above that. Need to buy before you sell? Ask about a bridge loan or HELOC on your current home for the down payment. Option 2: Remodel what you have Pros: Keep your neighborhood, rate and tax base. Spend only on what's missing. Cons: Living in a construction zone. Costs can drift. Over-improving for the street limits resale value. Financing options: HELOC: draw as you go; keeps your first mortgage untouched. Best when you have equity today. Fixed home equity loan: one lump sum at a fixed rate; predictable. Fannie Mae HomeStyle Renovation: borrow against the after-renovation value; renovation funds up to 75% of the as-completed value ( Fannie Mae ). Useful when your current equity is thin. FHA 203(k): Limited 203(k) now covers up to $75,000 in non-structural repairs; Standard 203(k) handles larger and structural projects ( HUD comparison ). Cash-out refinance: only when your current rate is already near today's rates. Option 3: Tear down and rebuild Pros: Exactly the house you want on land you already love. New systems, energy efficiency, and often more square footage. Cons: The longest timeline and largest budget. Carrying a rental and a construction loan at the same time. City approvals vary widely across the San Gabriel Valley. Financing options: Construction-to-permanent (one-time close): one loan funds the build in draws, then converts to a regular mortgage. Two-step construction loan: a short-term construction loan, then a separate mortgage at completion. More flexible, with two sets of closing costs. Land equity counts. If you own the lot free and clear or with low debt, that equity often covers the down payment. Checklist: which path fits you? Count your "yes" answers in each group. Lean toward buying if: You want a different school district, commute or neighborhood Your current mortgage rate is close to today's rates You need the space within six months You or your spouse are 55+ and Prop 19 lets you carry your tax base Lean toward remodeling if: You love the location

t: Inheriting Your Parents' California Home: Prop 19, Property Taxes, and Sibling Buyouts
c: How Prop 19's $1,044,586 exclusion works, the one-year deadlines, and how one sibling can buy out the others.
x: The short answer: Since February 16, 2021, a child who inherits a parent's California home keeps the parent's low property tax base only if the child moves in as their primary residence within a year, and only up to the parent's taxed value plus $1,044,586 (for transfers through February 15, 2027). Rentals and second homes no longer qualify. When one sibling keeps the house and buys out the others, the mortgage plan matters as much as the tax plan. What did Prop 19 change? Before 2021, parents could pass almost any California property to their children at the parents' tax base. Prop 19 narrowed that to the family home or family farm , and only when the child uses the home as their principal residence ( California BOE, Pub. 800-1 ). Rental properties, vacation homes and commercial buildings are now reassessed to market value on transfer. The exclusion is capped at the home's factored base year value plus an inflation-adjusted amount. The State Board of Equalization raised that amount to $1,044,586 for transfers from February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027 ( BOE news release ). Grandparent-to-grandchild transfers can qualify when the grandchild's parent has passed away. What does it look like in dollars? An example from the San Gabriel Valley, using a 1.25% effective tax rate (typical for Los Angeles County with local assessments): Assessed value Approximate annual tax Parents' current taxed value $300,000 $3,750 Child moves in, Prop 19 applies ($1.8M market value − $1,044,586) $755,414 $9,443 Child doesn't move in (full reassessment) $1,800,000 $22,500 Moving in saves roughly $13,000 a year in this example, even though the tax still rises. Your county assessor makes the actual determination. What are the deadlines? The child must make the home their principal residence within one year of the transfer. The child must file for the homeowners' exemption within one year , plus the BOE-19-P claim form (BOE-19-G for grandchildren). If the child later moves out, the exclusion ends and the home is reassessed. How do sibling buyouts work? This is the conversation I have most often. Three siblings inherit a $1.8 million home; one wants to live there. To buy out the other two, that sibling usually needs a loan: Inherited-property buyout financed as a rate-and-term refinance. Many lenders treat an estate or trust buyout as a purchase-like transaction rather than a cash-out, which can mean better pricing. Ask specifically. Loan amount. Buying out two-thirds of $1.8 million is about $1.2 million, which sits just under the 2026 Los Angeles County conforming limit of $1,249,125 ( FHFA via Calculated Risk ). Above that, it's a jumbo loan. Timing. Line up financing before the trust or probate distributes the property, so the transfer, the move-in and the refinance happen in the right order. Qualifying. The sibling who stays must qualify on their own income for the new payment plus the higher property tax. What should parents do now? Review your trust with an estate attorney. Distribution language matters under Prop 19; a trust doesn't preserve the exclusion automatically. Talk with your children about who, if anyone, wants to live in the home. Know your home's current taxed value. It's on your property tax bill. If no one will move in, compare keeping the home as a fully reassessed rental against selling. The math has changed. If you're 55 or older and want to move, Prop 19 may also let you carry your own tax base to a new home anywhere in California. That's a separate rule worth its own conversation. Derek\'s take In the San Gabriel Valley, the family home is often the family's largest asset and the center of multigenerational life. Prop 19 didn't end the ability to pass it down; it added deadlines and conditions. I work alongside estate attorneys and CPAs to make sure the financing fits the plan, and I'm glad to join a family meeting. Frequently asked questions Can I inherit my parents' rental property at their tax base? Not since February

t: Should You Pay Off Your Mortgage Early or Invest the Difference?
c: What an extra $500 a month really does at 3% vs. 6.75%, and the order of operations most families should follow.
x: The short answer: Your mortgage rate is the guaranteed return on every extra dollar you pay toward it. With a 3% loan, paying extra earns 3%, and many families do better keeping that money liquid or invested. With a rate near 7%, extra payments become a strong, risk-free return. Either way, fund your emergency cushion and retirement match first; only then decide between the two. What does an extra $500 a month actually do? Here is the same $500,000 balance with 25 years left, at two different rates, with $500 a month added to principal: Mortgage rate Monthly principal & interest Interest saved with +$500/mo Paid off early by 3.00% $2,371 $54,056 5.9 years 6.75% $3,455 $160,719 6.5 years Illustrative calculation using standard amortization: $500,000 balance, 300 months remaining, extra $500 applied to principal each month. Excludes taxes, insurance and any mortgage insurance. The extra dollars are the same. The payoff is three times larger at the higher rate because each dollar of principal you retire stops costing you 6.75% instead of 3%. When paying extra makes sense Your rate is higher than what you'd reliably earn elsewhere after taxes. You're within 10 to 15 years of retirement and want lower fixed expenses. You already have six months of expenses saved and are maxing employer retirement matches. The peace of mind of a paid-off home matters to you. That's a legitimate reason. When keeping the cash usually wins Your rate is around 3% to 4% and safe savings pay close to or above it. Your income is variable: commission, self-employment, the trades, or a job facing AI-driven change. You may need a down payment soon for a move-up home, a rental or a child's first home. You have higher-rate debt, such as car loans or credit cards, to pay off first. One point people overlook: extra principal doesn't lower your monthly payment. If income drops, money you put into the house helps only if you can borrow it back, and lenders approve HELOCs and refinances on current income. A middle path many of my clients use Build the cushion first: six months of housing costs in savings. Capture the free money: the full employer 401(k) or 403(b) match. Open a HELOC while your income is strong, and leave it unused as backup. Split what's left: some toward principal, some invested, based on your rate and how soon you'll need the money. Revisit when rates move. If rates fall below yours, refinancing may beat any extra-payment plan. What about the mortgage interest deduction? It can lower the effective cost of your mortgage if you itemize, but fewer households itemize than before. Ask your CPA what your after-tax rate really is. That's the number to compare against investments. Derek\'s take There's no single right answer, and anyone who says there is isn't looking at your numbers. I'm a mortgage broker, not a financial planner, so I'll show you the loan math clearly and work alongside your advisor on the rest. Send me your current statement and I'll run this table with your actual loan. Frequently asked questions Is it smart to pay off a 3% mortgage early? Usually it's not urgent. Most households benefit more from cash reserves and retirement savings first. Does paying extra each month shorten my loan? Yes, as long as the extra is applied to principal. Confirm with your servicer. Biweekly payments vs. one extra payment a year? They reach roughly the same result. Avoid paid biweekly programs; you can do it yourself for free. Should I refinance instead? If today's rate is meaningfully lower than yours and you'll stay long enough to recover closing costs, yes. Let's compare. This article is general information, not investment or tax advice. Consult a licensed financial advisor and CPA about your situation.
